claims.text: The Cantor alloy is an FCC high-entropy alloy.
A nanometric Cu interlayer in FCC HEA multilayers can induce a transition from diffusion-mediated creep to dislocation-mediated creep.
Copper has a lattice parameter nearly matched to that of the proposed FCC HEA.
Changing Cu interlayer thickness can tune interface coherency.
The Cu interlayer alters interfacial misfit strain between the HEA layers.
Changes in interface coherency and misfit strain alter available diffusion pathways.
Changes in interface coherency and misfit strain alter the ease of dislocation nucleation.
Very thin Cu layers produce highly coherent interfaces.
Highly coherent interfaces enhance atomic mobility along the boundary and favor diffusion-mediated creep.
Coble or Nabarro–Herring creep may operate in the thin-Cu-layer regime.
Increasing Cu layer thickness changes the interface from coherent to semi-coherent.
A semi-coherent interface facilitates stress concentration and dislocation nucleation.
The increased dislocation nucleation at semi-coherent interfaces switches the dominant creep mechanism to dislocation-mediated creep.
A critical Cu layer thickness and corresponding interface-coherency state exist at which creep activation energy and strain-rate behavior change.
Below the critical Cu thickness, creep will show higher diffusivity and a lower stress exponent consistent with diffusion-mediated creep.
Above the critical Cu thickness, creep will show a higher stress exponent and microstructural evidence of dislocation motion.
The proposed effect is limited to temperatures and stresses at which Cu remains stable without significant coarsening or phase transformation.
The proposed effect requires moderate lattice mismatch that permits interface coherency to be varied.
